study.title: Psalm 115 - Glory to God, contempt of idols and trust in the Lord
study.overview: This psalm radically contrasts the living God with empty idols. The community begins by refusing any credit to itself and asking that all glory go to the name of the Lord, for his goodness and faithfulness. Then it denounces the uselessness of idols, made by human hands and incapable of acting, speaking or aiding. Then the psalm calls all the people of God to trust in the Lord, reaffirms his promises of blessing and states that the God who created the heavens and the earth continues to act for his people. The closing recalls that the dead no longer praise, so that the living must bless the Lord now and forever.

outline.title: Glory belongs to the Lord, not to the people
outline.explanation: The psalm begins with a renunciation of boasting: the community does not want to itself the honor due to God. The question of the peoples Where is their God? It is answered with a confession of faith: the God of Israel is in heaven and acts according to his will.

outline.title: The uselessness of idols
outline.explanation: Idols are described as material objects, produced by human hands, lifeless and without the ability to perceive or respond. The conclusion is severe: both those who make them and those who trust in them become like them, that is, empty and incapable of true communion with the living God.

outline.title: Invitation to trust and certainty of blessing
outline.explanation: Israel, the house of Aaron, and all who fear the Lord are called to trust in him, because he is help and shield. The psalm responds to the apparent divine silence with the remembrance that the Lord remembers his people and blesses him, without distinction between small and great.

outline.title: The living must bless the Lord
outline.explanation: The Lord is exalted as Creator, owner of the heavens, while the earth was delivered to men for his present life. As the dead do not share in earthly praise, the proper response of the living is to bless the Lord continually, in permanent praise.

study.context: The text itself suggests a moment of pressure or mockery of the nations, for it mentions the ironic question: "Where is their God?" The psalm responds to this challenge with confession, contrast to idols and renewal of trust. The notes inform that many manuscripts and ancient versions unite this psalm with the previous one, but it is treated as a distinct psalm in Hebrew.
study.theology: The psalm teaches the centrality of God's glory and rejects all human self-glorification. Theologically, he affirms the sovereignty of the Lord: he is in heaven, possesses real authority, and acts according to his will. It also confronts idolatry as a lifeless religion, unable to see, hear, speak or save. Biblical trust is not abstraction: Israel, the house of Aaron, and all who fear the Lord are called to depend on him as help and shield. At the same time, the psalm binds the blessing to the character of God himself, who remembers his people and blesses him. Finally, he places praise on the horizon of the present life: while there is life, there is a duty and privilege to bless the Lord.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm is presented as a hymn of thanksgiving in which the community attributes all glory to the name of the Lord, a true source of hope and blessing.
The psalm excludes all boasting: any mercy received, service rendered or success achieved must be attributed entirely to God.
Idols are described as objects without life and without the ability to see, hear, feel, walk or speak; therefore, trusting in them is pure folly.

questions: In which areas of life do I still try to receive to me the glory that belongs only to the Lord?
What practical forms of modern idolatry can be competing with my trust in God?
If the psalm calls the living to bless the Lord, how can I make my praise more conscious, constant and communal?
study.practice: This week, practice three attitudes: reject any self-promotion in your words of prayer and witness; identify a functional "dovine" that is occupying the place of trust in God and abandons it; and set a moment to bless the Lord with concrete gratitude for his goodness and faithfulness. If you are in distress, use this psalm as a prayer: recognize the sovereignty of God, trust in it as a shield and respond to fear with praise.
study.uncertainty: The chapter does not safely inform the author, the exact occasion or a precise historical date. The notes suggest only a context of mockery or humiliation before the nations, but this remains inference, not explicit given the text. It is also not possible to determine for sure whether the psalm was originally composed independently or next to the previous psalm.
